title: Networked KV Cache Eviction Pressure - cross-sku comparison
content:
Summary:
This is a working doc for the networked KV-cache eviction-pressure experiment across representative cloud GPU SKUs (A100, H100, L40S). We focused on long-context prefills and mixed small/large decode traffic that stresses remote KV fetch paths (host ⇄ device, NVMe spill, and PCIe/NVLink transfer characteristics). Goal is to understand how SKU, driver, and CUDA stack interact with eviction churn and tail-latency under production-like mixes.

Key takeaways (short):
- H100 (recent driver) gives best p50/p95 for decode-heavy long-context workloads but shows higher instantaneous eviction churn when CUDA driver has aggressive preemption settings.
- A100 remains most stable under sustained multi-tenant small-batch loads; eviction rates lower when host-device transfer is host-pinned and large-prefetch is enabled.
- L40S produced surprisingly high eviction/reload IO when NVMe-backed KV spill was used on our cloud SKU; p99s spiked due to NVMe read amplification under concurrent background GC.
- Driver/CUDA stack: we observed an actionable regression on driver 535.x on H100 nodes (micro-stall bursts). Upgrading to 545.x reduced measured stall counts by ~30% in our environment.

Experimental context and motivation:
We have multiple customers hitting unpredictable p99s in long-context generation (prefill + decode) with per-customer KV caches deployed in host memory and an NVMe spill tier for very large convo histories. Classic routing options include: (1) keep everything on-device (when model fits), (2) host-resident KV cache with fast host-device copies, (3) NVMe spill for >host-memory cases. This experiment isolates scenario (2) and (3) across cloud SKUs to measure eviction pressure and its downstream impact.

Hypothesis:
- SKU interconnect (NVLink vs PCIe) and NVMe locality will dominate eviction-reload penalty for mixed traffic.
- Driver/CUDA behavior (context preemption, stream scheduling) can amplify short bursts of eviction churn into multi-100ms p99 spikes.

Testbed:
- Workloads: synthetic mix modeled from production traces: 60% small-chat (prefill 64 tokens, decode 64 tokens), 30% long-prefill (prefill 2048 tokens, decode 512 tokens), 10% bulk-embedding/utility (non-KV).
- Concurrency: 8 concurrent replicas per node, request mix applied uniformly.
- KV cache strategy: host-resident LRU with capacity tuned to nominal 6k key entries; NVMe spill enabled for overflow (direct-io reads).
- Models: 13B transformer variant (fast attention kernels), fixed config across SKUs to avoid model-level differences.
- SKUs tested (single-node):
  * GCP A100-40GB (n1-standard with PCIe link) — CUDA 11.8, driver 510.x baseline
  * AWS h100.8xlarge (H100 NVLink mesh) — CUDA 12.3, driver 535.x and 545.x tested
  * Azure L40S (L4S SKU) — CUDA 11.8, driver 525.x baseline (NVMe local storage configuration)
- Measurements: p50/p95/p99 latency (prefill, decode, end-to-end), eviction rate (evicts/min), reload IO (MB/s), NVLink/PCIe utilization, GPU occupancy, stall counters (probe via perf and nvprof traces), power draw (W) sampled at 1s.

Key metrics (representative numbers from runs - median across 5 repeat experiments):
- End-to-end p99 (ms) for long-prefill + decode:
  * A100: 320ms
  * H100 (driver 545.x): 270ms
  * L40S: 410ms
- Eviction rate (evicts/min at steady state):
  * A100: 18 evicts/min
  * H100: 26 evicts/min (535.x) -> 18 evicts/min (545.x)
  * L40S: 42 evicts/min
- NVMe read amplification (MB read per logical KB of cache miss):
  * A100 (no NVMe on host path): 1.2MB per KB-equivalent (low amplification due to host memory fallback)
  * H100: 1.4MB per KB-equivalent (NVLink batching reduces per-op overhead)
  * L40S: 6.8MB per KB-equivalent (high amplification due to concurrent GC + small IOs)
- p99 tail correlation with eviction bursts (observed Pearson r ~0.72 across samples)
- Power delta during heavy eviction bursts (avg additional draw):
  * A100: +15W
  * H100: +22W
  * L40S: +28W

Observations / narrative details:
1) Eviction churn mechanics on L40S:
   - L40S test nodes had local NVMe configured in a single partition used for KV spill. When eviction pressure rose, we observed many small random reads (4–16KB) rather than large batched reads. Background host-side garbage collector (cloud image agent) during one run coincided and caused NVMe IO queue depth saturation; read latencies jumped and decoded p99s shot up. Postmortem showed poor read coalescing on the spill layer (our host-side loader issues small aligned reads).
2) Driver sensitivity on H100:
   - Driver 535.x produced micro preemption bursts visible as short GPU stalls (4–20ms) during cross-device memcpy operations; end-to-end p99 pushed up. After upgrading to 545.x (and toggling scheduler flags to less aggressive preemption) stalls reduced and eviction-induced p99 dropped by ~15–25% depending on batch mix.
3) A100 stability:
   - A100 nodes had lower eviction rates due to host-pinned memory transfers being more predictable in our config and less NVMe dependency. When eviction did occur, the host->device path had higher throughput but slightly higher sustained power.
4) NVLink vs PCIe behaviour:
   - NVLink helped H100 amortize repeated KV loads (higher sustained throughput), provided the workload allowed batching; however, small-random reads still showed p99 penalties when eviction churn is random.

Repro steps (short):
- CI job name: perf/kv-eviction-sku-comparison. Key commands:
  1) deploy test harness (docker image: gcr.io/redwood/kv-test:v2025-11-01)
  2) ./run_bench --model 13b --mix workload-mix.json --nodes 1 --replicas 8 --kv-policy host-lru --kv-capacity 6000 --nvme-spill /mnt/kvspill --duration 30m
  3) collect traces: ./collect_traces --nvprof --iostat 1s --nvidia-smi 1s --powermon 1s --perf-sample
  4) aggregate: python tools/kv_agg.py --input traces/ --out results.json
- scripts and exact env are in linked_artifacts PR #398.

Immediate recommendations (actionable):
- Short term (low effort):
  * Add coalescing layer to host NVMe loader (batch small reads into 1MB linear reads). This reduced NVMe amplification in a Canary test by ~3x on L40S.
  * For H100 fleets, standardize on driver 545.x (or later after internal verification) and set preemption to conservative for inference nodes.
- Medium term (policy/architecture):
  * For very long-context workloads, prefer H100 fleet if customers need consistent p99s and are willing to accept slightly higher power usage — but gate by driver verification.
  * Rework spill policy: prefer larger, less-frequent spill writes and opportunistic prefetch of predicted next-chunk on warmup.
- Monitoring changes:
  * Add a KV eviction burst alert (evicts/min > 50 for >30s) tied to a queryable trace-id so SRE can triage NVMe GC vs driver stall source.
  * Surface per-node NVMe IO amplification metric on console.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does multi-node distributed KV (sharded) compare with host-local KV for these same mixes? (Tradeoffs: network cross-node vs NVMe amplification)
- Re-run L40S tests after disabling cloud image agent and using a separate partition with no background processes. Check if amplification drops.
- Validate with a 70B model variant (likely fewer cache hits due to larger keys) — will eviction profile change qualitatively?

Appendix — raw snippet of an interesting trace (abridged):
- trace id: run-2025-11-08-23:47
  * timeline: 00:00–00:15 steady state, 00:15–00:17 eviction burst (evicts/min jumped from 22 -> 120), 00:17–00:20 p99 spike to 1.2s
  * nvme iops: baseline 1800 IOPS -> burst 16k IOPS (4KB reads)
  * observed: host loader spawned many concurrent small reads, QD hit 128, nvme latency 8ms -> 120ms
  * mitigation taken mid-run: toggled coalescing in loader, QD dropped to 16, nvme latency fell to 12ms, p99 recovered to ~350ms

Notes to self (work items):
- Pete on SRE to isolate cloud image agent runs on a test partition and retest L40S (ticket created JIRA-8472).
- Push hotfix for host nvme loader to PR #398 and run canary across 3 L40S nodes.
- Add eviction-burst alert into console routing (owner: Daniel).

This doc is intentionally informal — contains experiment logs and working hypotheses. Will convert into a polished runbook if results hold after follow-ups.
